the Government wanted to meet he widely expressed desire of

except with some minor" differences. Both the Geneva Protocol
of 1923 and the Convention of 1927 were appended as Schedules
to this Act. So far as the ordinary arbitration law was concerned,
prior to the enactment of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940 there
were two sets of laws applicable to what were called Presidency
towns and areas which did not fall within those towns. Th~
Indian Arbitration Act, 1899 applied to cases where the subject
matter submitted to arbitration was of a nature that if a suit were
to be instituted it could be instituted in a Presidency town. Section
4(b) contained the definition of the word "submission" which
was similar to the definition in the English Act of 1889. In the
Civil Procedure Code of 1882 Part V dealt with arbitration.
These provisions were applicable to such areas which were out-side the Presidency towns. When the Civil Procedure Code, 1908
was enacted it contained in the IInd Schedule similar provisions
for arbitration. There was, however, no definition of
"submission" or "arbitration agreement". The Arbitration Act,
1940 was meant to consolidate and amend the law relating to
arbitration in India. The word "submission" was not defined but
the word "arbitration agreement" ins. 2(a) was stated to meav
a written agreement to submit present or future differences to
arbitration whether the arbitrator was named therein or not.
